intro: Every long story is heading somewhere. In this last unit you read how Michael Heiser understood the ending of the Bible's story. He read it as a family story. God has a heavenly family and a human family. Both had rebels. In Heiser's reading, the story ends with the two families restored together, the nations won back, and God dwelling with his people in a renewed Eden.

You will read the texts he built on: John 1 and 10, Romans 8, Galatians 4, 1 Corinthians 6, Psalm 82, Isaiah 14, and Revelation 16 and 20–22. You will weigh his boldest proposals, such as his reading of Har Magedon as the mount of assembly. Beside each one you will meet other readings: human judges in Psalm 82, Israel at Sinai in rabbinic writings, Eastern Orthodox theosis, Jewish readings of God's children, and four ways to read Revelation.

By the end you will be able to explain what Heiser argued about believers' destiny and why he said they never become equal to God. You will be able to trace a word from Hebrew into Greek, compare a symbol with its Hebrew Bible source, and describe a debate fairly without taking a side.
bigQuestion: How did Heiser read the end of the Bible's story, from God's family restored to the nations healed, and how do other readers understand the same texts?

timeline.t: Pharaoh Thutmose III wins a battle at Megiddo, recorded at Karnak
King Josiah of Judah dies at Megiddo facing Pharaoh Necho (2 Kings 23:29)
John 10 sets Jesus quoting Psalm 82:6 in the temple courts in Jerusalem
Paul writes 1 Corinthians, saying believers will judge angels
Paul writes Romans, with its chapter on adoption and creation's hope
Revelation is written, by many scholars' dating, naming Har Magedon
Athanasius writes On the Incarnation, a key text for theosis
Gregory Palamas distinguishes God's essence and energies
A battle near Megiddo in World War I takes the city's name
Heiser publishes The Unseen Realm, including his reading of Har Magedon
Michael Heiser dies, leaving his books and the Naked Bible Podcast

test.q: In Heiser's reading, what are God's two families?
choices: His heavenly family and his human family
test.why: Heiser described God's heavenly family and human family, meant to live together.

test.q: Which reading of Deuteronomy 32:8 did Heiser build on?
choices: The Qumran and Septuagint 'sons of God'
test.why: Heiser built on the older reading 'sons of God' found at Qumran and in the Septuagint.

test.q: What does John 1:12 say those who received him were given?
choices: The keys to the bottomless pit
Power, or the right, to become sons of God
test.why: John 1:12 says they were given power, or the right, to become the sons of God.
Romans 8:23 speaks of waiting for the adoption, the redemption of the body.

test.q: In 1 Corinthians 6:3, what does Paul say believers will do?
test.why: Paul asks, 'Know ye not that we shall judge angels?'

test.q: Which psalm does Jesus quote in John 10:34?
test.why: Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6, 'I said, Ye are gods.'

test.q: How does Orthodox theosis differ from becoming God?
choices: Humans replace God on his throne
Humans share God's life by grace, never his essence
test.why: Orthodox teaching says humans share God's energies by grace, never his essence.

test.q: Which verse calls Israel God's son, his firstborn?
test.why: Exodus 4:22 says Israel is God's son, his firstborn.

test.q: What limit did Heiser set on believers' destiny?
choices: They will be raised high but never equal to God
test.why: Heiser insisted that God alone is uncreated and unique in kind.

test.q: Why do some scholars doubt that Har Magedon means Mount Megiddo?
choices: Megiddo is a mound on a plain, never called a mountain
test.why: Megiddo is a tel on a plain, and no Hebrew Bible text calls it a mountain.

test.q: In Heiser's reading, where is the final battle really aimed?
choices: At God's mountain, Zion, the mount of assembly
test.why: Heiser read the battle as the powers' last stand against God's council mountain, Zion.

test.q: Which two place names show Greek writing ayin as g?
test.why: Hebrew 'Amorah and 'Azzah became Greek Gomorrha and Gaza.

test.q: What does Revelation 22:2 say the leaves of the tree of life are for?
test.why: Revelation 22:2 says the leaves are for the healing of the nations.

test.q: Which approach reads Revelation as timeless truths rather than particular events?
test.why: The idealist approach reads Revelation as pictures of timeless truths.

test.q: Which Hebrew Bible room shares the new Jerusalem's cube shape?
test.why: 1 Kings 6:20 gives the holy of holies equal length, width and height.

write.prompt: Heiser read the end of the Bible's story as God's family restored and the nations won back. Choose two or three passages from this unit (for example Psalm 82:6–8, 1 Corinthians 6:3, Revelation 3:21, Isaiah 14:13, Revelation 16:16 or 22:2). Explain what each says, how Heiser read it, and how at least one other reader or tradition reads it.
tips: Name each text by book, chapter and verse, and say which translation you used.
Attribute every reading: Heiser argues, many commentators read, Orthodox teaching says.
Compare readings side by side; do not rank them or say which is true.
Use the unit's terms, such as divine council, adoption, har mo'ed and theosis, and explain each one.
Describe Heiser's ideas in your own words; his books are not quoted.
